A_target.statement:
Let $\mathbf C$ be a [[Definition:Metacategory|category]].
A [[Definition:Morphism|morphism]] $m$ is a [[Definition:Monomorphism (Category Theory)|monomorphism]] {{iff}}:
:$\forall f, g: m \circ f = m \circ g \implies f = g$

B_source.statement:
Let $\mathbf C$ be a [[Definition:Metacategory|category]].
A [[Definition:Morphism|morphism]] $e$ is an [[Definition:Epimorphism (Category Theory)|epimorphism]] {{iff}}:
:$\forall f, g: f \circ e = g \circ e \implies f = g$

object_map.reformulation: Pass to the opposite category C^op, reversing every morphism.

validity_conditions: The cancellation property is stated purely via composition of arrows, so reversing all arrows turns right-cancellation into left-cancellation.
Op is an involution, so mono in C is exactly epi in C^op.
proof_plan: Write the [[Definition:Epimorphism (Category Theory)|epimorphism]] property as right-cancellation, using only composition.

Pass to $\mathbf C^{\text {op} }$, reversing every morphism.
This swaps the order of composition: $f \circ^{\text {op} } e = e \circ f$.
The reversed statement is left-cancellation, that is, the [[Definition:Monomorphism (Category Theory)|monomorphism]] property.

Hence $m$ is a monomorphism in $\mathbf C$ {{iff}} $m$ is an epimorphism in $\mathbf C^{\text {op} }$.
{{qed}}
